record.paper_title: Open questions in massive star research
record.original_question: Why do large spectroscopic surveys show a dearth of very young massive stars above about 20 solar masses in the Galaxy, the Large Magellanic Cloud, and the Small Magellanic Cloud? Are these stars still embedded in their birth clouds or still accreting for roughly half of their total lifetime, and if so why is the corresponding population of infrared-bright stars not observed?

evidence.quote: 2.3. Are young very massive stars embedded?

Perhaps, the missing stars are still embedded in their birth clouds or even accreting (cf., Sect. 2.1). However, to solve the problem, they need to remain hidden at optical wavelengths for roughly half their total lifetime, but a corresponding population of IR bright stars seems also not observed.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Large optical spectroscopic surveys of OB stars in the Milky Way, the Large Magellanic Cloud (LMC), and the Small Magellanic Cloud (SMC) reveal a statistically significant deficit of very young (near zero-age main sequence) massive stars with initial masses above roughly 20 solar masses, relative to the numbers expected from standard stellar evolution timescales combined with observed populations of more evolved O-type stars and the initial mass function inferred at lower masses.

Provide a quantitative explanation for this deficit. In particular, address the following hypothesis and its observational consequences:

(a) Suppose that very massive stars (M ≳ 20 M_⊙) remain embedded in their natal molecular clouds, or continue to accrete from them, for a fraction f of their main-sequence lifetime. Determine whether f must be of order 1/2 in order to reproduce the observed dearth of optically visible young very massive stars in the Galaxy, the LMC, and the SMC.

(b) Under the assumption that such an embedded/accreting phase exists with f ≈ 1/2, predict the expected number, spatial distribution, and infrared luminosity function of the corresponding population of infrared-bright, optically obscured very massive young stellar objects in each of these three galaxies, and reconcile this prediction with the apparent observational absence of such an IR-bright population.

(c) If hypothesis (a)–(b) is rejected, propose and quantitatively evaluate alternative mechanisms (e.g., delayed onset of optical visibility, rapid early mass growth, selection biases in spectroscopic surveys, or revised pre-main-sequence evolutionary tracks for M ≳ 20 M_⊙) that can simultaneously account for the optical deficit and the lack of a compensating infrared-bright young massive star population.
artifact.status_search_result: The question of the apparent absence of young, very massive (>20 M_⊙) stars near the zero-age main sequence in the Milky Way and Magellanic Clouds remains an active open problem in massive star formation research. Recent reviews and survey papers (e.g., VLT-FLAMES, BLOeM, ULLYSES/XShootU programs) continue to discuss the discrepancy without a consensus resolution; no embedded/IR-bright counterpart population accounting for ~half of their lifetimes has been confirmed.

status_evidence.title: Open questions in massive star research
status_evidence.snippet: Are young very massive stars embedded? ... a corresponding population of IR bright stars seems also not observed.
status_evidence.claim: The deficit of young very massive stars and the absence of a matching IR-bright population are identified as unresolved open questions.

status_evidence.title: BLOeM: A spectroscopic survey of massive stars in the SMC
status_evidence.snippet: We confirm a relative paucity of very young, very massive stars compared to expectations from standard evolutionary models.
status_evidence.claim: Recent SMC spectroscopic surveys continue to report the dearth of young very massive stars, indicating the issue is still open.
